drafts.after: Wisdom speaks as one who already existed before creation. First principle: Proverbs 8 pictures Wisdom as a person, and John 1 and Colossians 1 are the background music of that chapter — the Son is the Wisdom by whom God made everything.

AFTER explains both terms in place and keeps the chapter citations and the claim that the Son is the wisdom by whom all was made exactly as strong.

drafts.after: God sees evil and good alike. First principle: God sees everything — no deed escapes the eyes that Hebrews says are open before the One with whom we have to do, the God we must answer to.
drafts.reason: BEFORE used the abstract label "total surveillance is God's attribute" and added "which Hebrews says" as a second idea inside one sentence. AFTER says plainly that God sees everything and that no deed escapes him, and glosses the KJV phrase "with whom we have to do" (Hebrews 4:13) in the same sentence. No quotation marks are put around the clause, so no KJV wording is altered or claimed.

drafts.after: Wisdom already existed before the earth did. First principle: living forever belongs to God alone, yet here Wisdom says it about herself. The early teachers of the church read this as the Son's eternal generation, which means the Son has always existed with the Father.
drafts.reason: BEFORE used the abstract label "Wisdom antedates the earth" and dropped the technical phrase "eternal generation" on the reader with no explanation, jammed into one em-dash sentence of 38 words. AFTER keeps the term but glosses it in the next sentence, and keeps the claim that this is how the fathers read the verse.

drafts.after: The fool repeats his folly. First principle: the warning here is a man who goes back to his old sin and is never made new. Peter quotes the dog, and he adds the washed sow, so the problem is the nature and not the habit.
drafts.reason: BEFORE invented the compressed noun "folly-repeat" and the abstract "relapse without re-creation", and chained three clauses with dashes. AFTER gives the warning a subject and a verb, keeps Peter's dog and washed sow unchanged in substance, and splits the dash-joined run into three sentences of 5, 21 and 24 words. The gate only splits at . ! ? and counts an em-dash run as one sentence, so the dash form had measured 37 words against the 35-word limit. The warning is not softened.

drafts.after: Do not lean on your own understanding. First principle: the lean of your heart is the whole matter — you trust God with all your weight or you do not trust him at all. Your own understanding is the other crutch you want to lean on.
drafts.reason: BEFORE turned the command into a statement ("Lean not on your own understanding") and left "the heart-lean" and "the rival crutch" as things to decode. AFTER says plainly that you either lean your whole weight on God or you do not trust him, and finishes with two short sentences instead of a dash-chained one.

drafts.after: Your heart shows itself in how you see others. First principle: you come to know your own heart by looking at how you see other people, and this proverb keeps testing you.
drafts.reason: BEFORE piled up hyphened compounds ("self-knowledge is mirror-knowledge", "heart's reflection", "standing audit"). AFTER keeps the mirror idea in plain words and says the same thing: what you see in others shows you your own heart, and the proverb is a constant test.

drafts.after: If God repays the righteous here on earth, what will he do to the wicked? First principle: God's judgment starts with his own people, and Peter quotes this same argument when he speaks of where the sinner will end up.
drafts.reason: BEFORE compressed the sentence into "If the righteous are recompensed here, how much more the wicked" and left "the much-more logic of the sinner's fate" as an abstract label. AFTER states the question in full, says judgment starts with God's own people, and keeps Peter and the citation unchanged.

drafts.after: Wine is for the person who is dying and for the one whose heart is heavy; it is a mercy, not a way of life. First principle: this proverb gives strong drink only to the perishing, so it quietly forbids it for judges and kings.
drafts.reason: BEFORE stacked "the heavy-hearted dying" and the invented label "a mercy-analgesic" into one dash clause. AFTER names the two kinds of people in ordinary words, keeps the same two claims, and does not soften the implied prohibition for judges and kings.

drafts.after: God scorns the scorners, and he gives grace to the lowly. First principle: James and Peter both quote this proverb word for word to show that the humble are the ones who receive grace.
drafts.reason: BEFORE used the abstract label "the grace-gradient proverb" and "to install humility as the grace-receiver". AFTER keeps the same quotation claim (James and Peter quote it word for word) and says plainly who receives grace.

drafts.after: The people curse the judge who calls the wicked righteous. First principle: a court that calls wickedness righteous brings a curse on the nation, and this proverb is the people's own verdict on judges who bend the law.
drafts.reason: BEFORE was a subjectless fragment ("The people curse the moral flip") with the invented compound "verdict-benders". AFTER names the judge who calls the wicked righteous, and keeps the same claim about the curse on the nation.

drafts.after: No one can say he has made his own heart clean. First principle: this question has only one answer, because cleaning a heart takes the One who made the heart. John names the man who claims he has done it as the one who deceives himself.
drafts.reason: BEFORE used "the rhetorical impossibility of self-purification" and "the self-deceiver" as abstract labels. AFTER keeps the point that the question is asked so that its one answer is obvious, keeps the Creator-of-the-heart claim, and keeps the apostle John naming the man who claims otherwise. The citation form "1 John" is not used in the rewrite, so no citation is added, dropped or renumbered.

drafts.after: The person who keeps God's law is happy, and that is the other road, the one that leads away from chaos. First principle: without a vision God has given, a people who rule themselves fall apart, and the book of Judges and Isaiah's straying sheep give the same diagnosis.
drafts.reason: BEFORE used the abstract labels "unrestraint", "Judges' refrain" and "Isaiah's sheep-stray". AFTER says what happens when a people rule themselves without God's revealed vision and spells out both references, keeping the claim and the same two passages.

drafts.after: Correction proves that you are a son, and giving up in weariness is forbidden. First principle: Hebrews quotes this proverb twice to change how we see suffering, and the child who is corrected is the child who truly belongs.
drafts.reason: BEFORE compressed the verse into "sonship-proof" and said Hebrews "reframes" suffering. AFTER keeps the command not to grow weary as a command, keeps the claim that Hebrews quotes it twice, and says plainly that the corrected child is the one who belongs.

drafts.after: Doing justice matters more to God than the offerings you bring to his altar. First principle: Samuel, Isaiah, Hosea and Jesus all teach that mercy pleases God more than sacrifice.
drafts.reason: BEFORE opened with the noun stack "Justice outweighs altar-traffic" and the label "the mercy-over-sacrifice proverb". AFTER states the comparison in a full sentence, names the same four witnesses, and adds no citation.

drafts.after: The lamp of the man who curses his parents goes out in thick darkness. First principle: when a child despises his father or mother, his light is put out. Exodus commands death for that sin, and this proverb turns the command into the picture of a snuffed lamp.
drafts.reason: BEFORE used "parental contempt" and "the lamp-out image" as abstract nouns and chained two ideas with a dash. AFTER names the child who curses his parents, keeps the Exodus death penalty claim unchanged, and keeps the lamp image. The run after "First principle:" is split at the point where the subject changes, so the gate (which splits only at . ! ?) measures 13, 20 and 23 words instead of one 35-word sentence that left no margin.
